overview: The Abbasids built an empire centred on Iraq after overthrowing the Umayyads in 750. Baghdad and Samarra became great centres of government, trade, craftsmanship and learning. The atlas supplies broad polygons only for 800 to 1000, which cannot represent uniform control. This card follows the Baghdad-based dynasty from 750 to 1258 through centuries of changing power.

periods.title: Revolution and Baghdad
periods.summary: A new dynasty established its capital at Baghdad in 762.

periods.title: The Samarra court
periods.summary: The caliphal capital moved to a newly built city on the Tigris.

periods.title: Baghdad and regional rulers
periods.summary: The court returned to Baghdad as provincial dynasties gained autonomy.

periods.title: Caliphs under stronger dynasties
periods.summary: Buyid and then Seljuq rulers dominated Baghdad while Abbasid religious authority continued.

periods.title: Renewal and Mongol conquest
periods.summary: Late Abbasid patronage revived before the Mongol capture of Baghdad.

items.text: The dynasty emerged from a revolution against Umayyad rule. After years of fighting, the last eastern Umayyad caliph was killed in 750. The new rulers initially based themselves at Kufa in Iraq, shifting the political centre away from Damascus before Baghdad existed.

Al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 as a carefully planned circular city. Four principal gates led toward a centre containing palace and mosque; homes, workshops and markets occupied the surrounding ring. The design made the ruler’s position visible in the city itself, connecting political power with the layout of streets and buildings.

By the tenth century, powerful regional dynasties were taking control of provinces. Buyids entered Baghdad in 945 and Seljuqs in 1055. The Abbasid caliph could retain religious prestige while another ruler commanded the army. A coloured imperial map therefore hides changing layers of authority.

The Mustansiriyya college, built in Baghdad between 1228 and 1233, provided a setting for the four main Sunni schools of law. Its foundation belongs to a late Abbasid revival of patronage. Learning institutions still expanded long after the dynasty had lost much of its original political reach.

sections.title: Water, toilets and the dinner table

items.text: At Samarra, the contemporary writer al-Ya’qubi described water carriers bringing drinking water from the Tigris in skin bags on pack animals. Wells were deep and their water could be salty. Supplying a household meant regular carrying and delivery: turning on a kitchen tap was not an option.

Excavated Samarra houses often arranged rooms around a courtyard. Drains, cisterns and basins suggest work such as washing clothes, cleaning and preparing food. In the small excavated sample, researchers found no connection to a city-wide piped supply; households managed water within their own buildings.

Some Samarra houses had private toilets and bathing rooms, identified partly through waterproof bitumen on their floors and walls. Their baths lacked the underfloor heating found in public baths. Archaeologists can learn about bathroom arrangements from humble waterproofing, even when almost everything else has vanished.

In tenth-century Baghdad, Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq compiled more than 620 recipes alongside stories, poems, table manners and handwashing preparations. A surviving manuscript even pairs an open-faced sandwich recipe with a poem about it. The book celebrates wealthy dining rather than documenting every family’s supper, but somebody clearly thought lunch deserved poetry.

A ninth-century tile excavated at Samarra shows how potters made clay shimmer like costly stone. They glazed and fired it, added metallic pigments, fired it again and polished the surface. This surviving fragment records careful control of materials and heat, giving a palace glitter without building every wall from precious stone.

Al-Khwarizmi presented algebra as useful for inheritance, trade, lawsuits, land measurement and canals. His ninth-century book explained calculations in words, without today’s familiar x symbols. Its geometry could turn an equation into areas of squares and rectangles: doing the maths also meant understanding a picture.

One example asks for a square that, added to ten times its side, makes thirty-nine. A side of three works: nine plus thirty equals thirty-nine. Al-Khwarizmi explained a general procedure for such problems, so a reader could solve another example rather than merely remember this answer.

Baghdad’s medical learning drew on Greek, Persian-Mesopotamian and Indian traditions. Muslim, Jewish and Christian scholars worked on texts in Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq’s translation workshop was particularly influential, while his Questions on Medicine organised knowledge for learners. This achievement depended on translators and collaborators as well as wealthy patrons.

Paper helped books circulate more widely. The National Library of Medicine links its introduction with the growth of reading materials and large medical compilations. Copying, organising and explaining information became major kinds of work; a useful scientific inheritance needed people who could keep it readable.

A medical manuscript dated 1224 includes an imagined scene of medicine-making, with vessels, a large cauldron and a waiting figure. The Met attributes it to Baghdad or northern Jazira. Its teaching guide describes pharmacy skills passing from father to son, supplemented by books. It reveals apprenticeship and beliefs about remedies, not proof that each treatment worked.

A marble tombstone from Egypt, dated 859, begins in Arabic: “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم”. The British Museum translates this as “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.” Its Kufic inscription remembers Ya’qub, son of ‘Abdullah. The sample is a transcription of actual Abbasid-period carving, bringing an individual life into the imperial story.

ending.text: Mongol forces captured Baghdad in 1258, ending Abbasid rule there. Abbasid caliphs later continued in Mamluk Egypt with largely nominal authority. The loss of the Baghdad dynasty did not end Arabic scholarship, crafts or the lives of its former subjects; political institutions and centres of patronage changed.
